sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About NGS Testing
sectionToMerge.intro: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) testing helps doctors read many cancer-related genes at once to guide more personalised treatment. These answers explain what NGS testing is, how it works, and how patients can access it.

items.a: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) testing is an advanced laboratory method that reads many cancer-related genes at once from a tumour or blood sample. It helps identify mutations, gene fusions, and other biomarkers that may guide targeted therapy or immunotherapy decisions. NGS gives doctors a detailed genetic profile of the cancer, which may support more personalised treatment. Results should always be interpreted by a qualified oncology team alongside the patient's full clinical picture.

items.q: How is NGS testing different from single-gene testing?
items.a: NGS testing differs from single-gene testing by analysing hundreds of genes simultaneously rather than one at a time. Single-gene tests look for a specific known mutation, while NGS provides a broad genomic profile in one run, often using less tissue and less time. This wider view may reveal actionable biomarkers that focused single tests could miss. The most suitable testing approach depends on cancer type, available tissue, and specialist recommendation.

items.q: What can NGS testing detect in cancer?
items.a: NGS testing can detect a wide range of genetic alterations, including point mutations, insertions, deletions, gene fusions, copy number changes, and markers like tumour mutational burden (TMB) and microsatellite instability (MSI). These findings may point to eligibility for targeted drugs or immunotherapy. However, not every detected alteration has a matching treatment, and results should be discussed with a qualified oncology team before any treatment decision is made.

groups.title: How NGS Testing Works and Who It Helps

items.a: NGS testing works by extracting DNA or RNA from a tumour tissue sample or a blood (liquid biopsy) sample, then sequencing millions of genetic fragments in parallel. Specialised software compares these sequences against reference genomes to detect mutations, fusions, and other alterations. A molecular pathologist reviews the findings and prepares a report. Turnaround usually takes one to three weeks, though timing depends on the laboratory, sample quality, and test complexity.

NGS testing may be considered for patients with advanced, metastatic, or hard-to-treat cancers, or when standard treatment options are limited. It may be suitable for selected patients with lung, colorectal, breast, ovarian, or other cancers where biomarkers guide therapy, and can also help when the primary cancer site is unknown. Whether NGS testing is appropriate depends on cancer type, stage, previous treatment, overall health, and the treating oncology team's assessment.

items.q: What sample is needed for NGS testing?
items.a: NGS testing usually requires either a tumour tissue sample from a biopsy or surgery, or a blood sample known as a liquid biopsy. Tissue testing is often preferred when enough good-quality sample is available, while liquid biopsy may help when tissue is limited or difficult to obtain. The best sample type depends on cancer type, tumour location, and laboratory requirements, and should be decided by the treating medical team.

items.q: How much does NGS testing cost and is it available in India?
items.a: The cost of NGS testing varies widely depending on the laboratory, the number of genes tested, sample type, and country. Broad comprehensive panels generally cost more than smaller, focused panels. In India, NGS testing is available at several accredited laboratories, often at more affordable rates than in many Western countries. Final pricing depends on the specific panel, hospital, diagnosis, and any additional tests advised by the treating team.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with NGS testing?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organise medical reports, identify laboratories or specialists offering NGS testing, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, sample logistics, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health. CancerFax supports coordination and does not replace the assessment or advice of the treating doctors and hospitals.
